Clonidine for portal hypertension: a sympathetic solution? Ann Intern Med 1992; 116: 515–17. Varicose veins. Varicose veins are tortuous, protruding veins in the legs, that occur when weak vein walls and valve incompe- tence result in venous reflux and dilatation. Symptoms associat- ed with varicose veins include heaviness, tension, aching, and itching of the legs. Complications include oedema, thrombophle- bitis, deep venous thrombosis, lipodermatosclerosis, and venous ulceration. Risk factors for varicose veins include increasing age, pregnancy, and occupations that involve prolonged standing.1 The management of varicose veins has been reviewed.1-3 Con- servative management using compression hosiery may be effec- tive for relief of symptoms in some patients but longer-term com- pliance is poor.3 Surgery or sclerotherapy are other treatment options, depending on the veins affected. Surgical treatment, which is the gold standard for treatment of more severe varicose veins, may involve ligation of the affected vein
